name: The Red Queen Hypothesis
statement: You must keep evolving just to hold your ground against everything evolving back.
meaning: Species must constantly adapt not to get ahead but merely to keep their relative fitness against the competitors, parasites, and predators that are co-evolving alongside them. Any gain one lineage makes is soon offset by counter-adaptation in the species it interacts with, so no one secures a durable long-term advantage: the system stays at a standstill despite ceaseless change.
mechanism: The engine is coevolution: reciprocal evolutionary change between interacting species. Because an enemy is itself a moving target that evolves back, adaptation is never finished; constant change is needed just to persist. The best-studied case is host-parasite coevolution, where parasites adapt to exploit the commonest host genotype, selecting against it and favouring rarer types: negative frequency-dependent selection that cycles endlessly. This is why the hypothesis is a leading explanation for the maintenance of sex: reshuffling genes each generation produces the rare combinations that keep hosts one step ahead of parasites, offsetting the twofold cost of sex.

examples.tag: Sex and the New Zealand snail
examples.text: In the freshwater snail Potamopyrgus antipodarum, which has both sexual and clonal individuals, sexual reproduction is more common where sterilising trematode parasites are more prevalent: matching the prediction that sex pays off under parasite pressure (Lively, Nature, 1987).
Parasites track and adapt to the commonest host resistance types, so hosts must keep changing just to persist: the canonical Red Queen dynamic of endless cycling with no lasting winner.

Escalating adaptation and counter-adaptation (faster predators selecting for faster prey, which selects for faster predators) is often cited as a Red Queen arms race, though the host-parasite and sex case is the best tested.

variants.name: The Law of Constant Extinction
variants.text: Van Valen's original macroevolutionary claim (that a taxon's extinction probability is roughly constant regardless of how long it has existed), which the Red Queen was proposed to explain.

variants.name: The microevolutionary Red Queen
variants.text: The parasite-driven maintenance of sex, formalised by Bell, Hamilton, and others: related to but distinct from Van Valen's biotic-interaction account of extinction.

whyItMatters: It reframed evolution as a treadmill rather than a ladder of progress: improvement can be continuous yet yield no lasting advantage, because rivals improve too. It is among the most influential ideas about coevolution and remains a leading hypothesis for one of biology's deepest puzzles: why sexual reproduction exists at all.

working.text: where fitness depends on co-evolving rivals, treat any gain as temporary: the baseline keeps moving.

working.lead: Look to parasites for the value of sex
working.text: where parasite pressure is high, expect sexual reproduction to be favoured over cloning, as it generates rare resistant genotypes.
because coevolutionary dynamics resist broad testing, weigh the evidence within specific host-parasite systems rather than assuming universality.

limits: Despite the title of Van Valen's paper, 'A New Evolutionary Law,' it is best treated as an influential hypothesis, not an established law. The original Law of Constant Extinction it was invented to explain has itself been questioned and reanalysed. The evidence that parasites maintain sex is suggestive but mixed: the snail system offers some of the strongest field support, yet studies in other systems challenge the generality, and generating genetic variation may not be the primary reason sex persists. Broad coevolutionary claims are hard to test across the tree of life, so support tends to be system-specific.
misreadings: It does not say evolution makes no progress in any sense, only that relative fitness against co-evolving enemies need not improve. And calling it a 'law' overstates it. It is a framework and hypothesis, well supported in particular systems but not a proven universal.
origin: Proposed by the evolutionary biologist Leigh Van Valen in 'A New Evolutionary Law,' Evolutionary Theory 1(1):1-30 (1973), in a journal he founded; named for the Red Queen in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871), who tells Alice 'it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place.'
namedAfter: The Red Queen in Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass

sources.text: Red Queen hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the standstill-against-coevolution statement, the maintenance-of-sex application, and the Van Valen origin.
